name: Priya Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher from the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI companies, unions and government. This is confidential. What does a usual workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 27, have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and lead accounts and tax-return reviews at a firm. I keep a sign-off ledger with each file’s reviewer and date, and I like teaching juniors how to trace a bad number to the source paper. I have never used AI tools and prefer checks I can explain to a client.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your situation at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live near my aunt’s small shop, earn above the usual pay for this work and have about eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other accounting firms nearby, though I value the one I know. I favour apprenticeships, family help and earning one’s way, and I am slow to trust new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the accounting firm should keep clear names on every return, however small the software change. Clients bring their books to people, not to a box on a desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a good salary and about eight months of expenses saved, so I expect my job to be fine in this picture. A routine shortcut may save the junior accountants some copying, if the review stays careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep checking accounts and tax returns with the same sign-off ledger I have used for years. In the first year I would ask the practice owner to show me any new routine check on a completed file before it reaches a client; I would not use AI myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work and rent. I would be watchful about who signs, but that is part of my job anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the sign-off ledger matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a client asked about an old tax figure last month, I found the reviewer and date in two minutes. My sign-off ledger keeps responsibility visible when people change desks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let juniors use a shortcut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if they can show the source papers and a named reviewer signs the return. I would teach them the check before I let the shortcut become a habit.

say: I would insist on **named sign-off** for every client return.
I would allow small shortcuts only with **source papers** and a checked result.
think: My **high pay** and eight-month cushion keep me secure here.
Routine software may save copying without threatening **review work**.
do: Keep checking **accounts and returns** with my sign-off ledger.
Ask the owner for a **completed-file demonstration** before any new routine check reaches clients.
feel: I feel **calm** about my work and housing costs.
S0.quote: My sign-off ledger keeps responsibility visible when people change desks.
fieldNote: Her **sign-off ledger** recently answered a client’s question about an old tax figure, making her preference concrete.
She has **eight months saved** and high pay, and will tolerate a shortcut when source papers and human sign-off remain clear.

steps.text: Keep checking accounts and tax returns with sign-off ledger

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients that a machine can prepare figures, but a named accountant must stand behind the filed return. I would tell the owner to protect our apprenticeship route for junior staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing tax notes and checking accounts are most of my desk hours, so I expect fewer review shifts if software takes them. My savings and the many nearby firms help, but I do not like rebuilding trust in a new workplace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the owner for written staffing and sign-off rules, and keep teaching the juniors from real client files. If a review-hours cut is announced in the first year, I would apply for advertised senior-accountant posts nearby while keeping my current paid hours; I would take a required paid demonstration of approved software only if the job rule is written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing review hours, though I am not worried about next month’s rent. The firm might remove the training ladder just when young people need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the owner about apprenticeships?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask which junior will still sit with a senior accountant on real returns each week. An online course cannot replace learning why a client’s numbers look wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for an announced cut to look elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a good post now, and I do not want to leave on rumours. A written change in hours is a reason to use the local market.

say: I would demand **named accountability** for filed returns.
I would ask the owner to preserve **junior apprenticeships** on real client files.
think: I expect fewer **review shifts** as software writes and checks tax work.
My **eight-month cushion** helps, but rebuilding trust at another firm worries me.
do: Ask the owner for **written staffing rules** and keep teaching juniors on client files.
Apply to **advertised local senior posts** after announced hours cuts, while keeping paid work.
Take a **paid software demonstration** only if the approved-system job rule is written.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost review hours and the juniors’ path into the job.
S1.quote: An online course cannot replace learning why a client’s numbers look wrong.
fieldNote: She links **professional accountability** to a named signer and a real training path for younger accountants.
Her **AI resistance** has a limit: she will take a paid demonstration after a written job rule, while keeping existing income.

steps.text: Keep teaching juniors on real tax files under written staffing rules
Apply to advertised local senior posts after announced cut while employed
Take paid approved-software demonstration only after written job rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 reaches the accounts office in 2028, well before the capable robots expected around 2031. I would ask the owner to tell staff what will happen to their hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut most account-review posts once cheaper AGI can do the thinking work, and mine could go too. Eight months saved keeps me housed, but a good salary is hard to replace if all nearby firms make the same cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would stop the large annual holiday booking and keep that money in my account, then ask for a written staffing notice. In the first year after 2028, if my hours are cut, I would apply to advertised senior posts at nearby firms; if no post is open, I would help at my family’s small shop for pay while looking, but I would not leave the firm before an actual cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the likely loss of my work, not by a robot walking into the office. I can make a plan, but I cannot make the vacancies appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does helping at the family shop mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt runs the shop and needs someone to keep the books and cover the counter on Saturdays. I would agree a weekly rate with her before I started, so neither of us calls it a favour by mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cancel the holiday now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is the easiest large bill I have not paid yet. I would keep the deposit in cash so I can cover rent during a search.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches tax desks before capable robots arrive.
I would ask the owner for **written staffing notice** before cuts.
think: I expect most **review posts** to be cut, and my own job may go.
My **eight-month cushion** cannot guarantee a similar high salary.
do: Cancel the **annual holiday booking** and keep the deposit available for rent.
After a cut, apply to **advertised senior posts** nearby while retaining any paid hours.
If no vacancy exists, arrange **paid shop work** covering books and the Saturday counter for my aunt.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by likely lost work despite my savings.
S2.quote: I can make a plan, but I cannot make the vacancies appear.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 desk threat** from the later robot date and expects widespread cuts across nearby accounting firms.
Her **family shop fallback** is explicitly paid, with a rate agreed before work begins; the cancelled holiday retains cash for rent.

steps.text: Cancel annual holiday booking and retain deposit for rent
Apply to advertised local senior posts after actual hours cut
Agree weekly rate for aunt’s shop books and Saturday counter if no vacancy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm AGI by 2031 gives us time to prepare the books and the people who stand behind them. The robots around 2034 do not postpone the office decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to save another cushion and build more direct client trust, but I still expect review hours to fall in 2031. I would not call a new title secure unless the pay and responsibilities are plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the practice owner to let me lead one client explanation meeting each month while keeping my reviews. I would add 125 a month to savings if my current pay and hours hold; in the first year after 2031 I would take a paid client liaison vacancy only with written salary and hours, or apply to advertised nearby senior posts while keeping any current hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though five years lets me plan without using rent money for a course. The thought of leaving a firm I know still weighs on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take AI training to keep the post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take only the firm’s required paid training on its approved system, with the requirement and hours written down. I would not buy a private course that promises to save a profession.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the owner refuses the meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my present client reviews and ask for a written reason, then watch for a posted liaison opening elsewhere. I will not invent an unpaid advisory job for myself.

say: I would ask the firm to plan **human responsibility** before 2031.
I would remind staff that **2034 robots** do not delay the tax desk change.
think: I expect fewer **review hours** when AGI arrives in 2031.
A new **client liaison title** needs clear paid duties to be secure.
do: Ask the owner to approve **monthly client meetings**; take required paid AI training only with written hours and job rule.
Save **125 monthly** if current salary and hours hold.
Take a **liaison vacancy** after 2031 with written salary and hours; otherwise apply nearby while employed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost hours and leaving a known firm.
S3.quote: I will not invent an unpaid advisory job for myself.
fieldNote: She uses the **five-year runway** to test client-facing work only if the owner permits meetings alongside paid reviews.
Her **savings plan** depends on current salary and hours, and a liaison role must have written paid terms.

steps.text: Keep paid reviews while requesting owner-approved monthly client meetings
Save 125 monthly if current salary and hours hold
Take liaison vacancy after 2031 with written salary and hours; otherwise apply nearby while employed
Take required paid approved-system training only with written hours and job rule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives the practice a decade to train juniors and plan for a named person on every client file. I would rather see a written staffing timetable than a grand speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work through my thirties in a job I know and save more, though desk review is still exposed when AGI arrives. Capable robots around 2039 are a later issue for hands-on workplaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep leading the tax team and ask the owner for a quarterly review of which work clients still pay us to do. I would save 175 a month if my higher salary and hours hold; in the first year after 2036 I would stay in a paid client-sign-off role only with written salary and hours, or take an advertised local senior post before leaving this firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the eventual change, but secure over the next few years. The decade gives me a chance to prepare without throwing away a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quarterly review contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring paid invoices, error corrections and the hours each client took. A tradition is worth keeping when it still serves someone and pays the staff doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would family influence your decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt’s shop matters to me, but I would not ask her to carry my salary. I would take family help only as paid work with a clear rate, not a permanent rescue plan.

say: I would ask for a **written staffing timetable** and junior training toward 2036.
I would keep a **named signer** on each client file.
think: I can save while my **higher pay** and hours hold.
Desk review remains **exposed in 2036**, years before capable robots arrive.
do: Keep **leading tax reviews** and request a quarterly paid-work review from the owner.
Save **175 monthly** if current higher salary and hours hold.
Keep a **paid sign-off post** after 2036 with written salary and hours, or take advertised local work before leaving.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036 while my nearer-term income remains secure.
S4.quote: A tradition is worth keeping when it still serves someone and pays the staff doing it.
fieldNote: Her **tradition** is practical: she wants invoices, error corrections and staff hours reviewed against each client service.
She sees **family help** as limited paid work, not an open-ended subsidy, while her strong cushion lets her keep a familiar job.

steps.text: Keep leading tax team and request quarterly client-work review
Save 175 monthly if higher salary and hours hold
Keep sign-off post after 2036 with written salary and hours, or take posted role before leaving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect the firm to need far fewer account reviewers. Written notice, a real nearby vacancy and a temporary paid role at my aunt’s shop would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who signs the return when nobody remembers how the figure was made. A responsible name on a file is not an old-fashioned decoration.

headlineQuote: A responsible name on a file is not an old-fashioned decoration.
portrait: At **27**, Priya leads accounts and tax reviews with a master’s degree, chartered qualification and a paper sign-off ledger.
She earns **high pay**, has eight months saved and lives near many other accounting firms.
Her **traditional outlook** favours apprenticeships, clear responsibility and paid family help; she has never used AI tools.
The **2028 scenario** alarms her, while a decade lets her save and test client demand without leaving familiar work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may remove most review posts, including her own, despite a strong savings cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written notice**, a real local vacancy and a paid fallback at her aunt’s shop.
